utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Naumann.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your cross-examination by Mr. Ackerman will now continue. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I hope the wasting away on the Bench is not a comment on my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were warned, but we are happy to arrange a special sitting until 7.00 this evening if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think there will be a necessity for that, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I told you we'd go back to this today, and here we go. Page 76, line 18, yesterday I asked you this question: "Why on earth then did NATO explain to persons that were interested in this that the reason they bombed from 15.000 was to keep their pilots from being hit by anti-aircraft and missiles." Your answer was: "I don't know who you are quoting. In our deliberations on the military side of NATO, this aspect that you've mentioned was not a decisive element." And I may not be listening to you well yesterday. You're not saying that's not true just that on the military side at least it was not a decisive element. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the military side would have included people like you and General Clark and General Short and people of that ilk; correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily, of course, General Short who was responsible for running the air operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. From General Clark's book at page 183, this is what he says to us: "As we start working through this, there are three majors of merit for the operation overall from the military standpoint. The first major of merit is not to lose aircraft, minimise the loss of aircraft. This addressed Mike Short's biggest concern to prevent the loss of air crews" . So that loss of aircraft and air crews, according to General Clark, was their number one major of merit. Do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why should I disagree with a statement of General Clark, but I repeat in the deliberations at NATO headquarters it was not a priority anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what the -- do you know what Defence Data Limited is?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's an organisation that publishes information for the defence community. In one of their articles in December 1999, they said: "During the air campaign," referring to Kosovo, "the requirement for allied manned aircraft to stay above 15.000 for reasons of safety helped deconfliction." The Crimes of War organisation said: "In order to evade Serbian anti-aircraft defences, NATO pilots made their bombing runs at high altitude, usually at or above 15.000 feet and at night." Human Rights Watch in a letter to General Solana, talking about rules of engagement of NATO: "These rules raised questions about the conduct of NATO's bombing in light of its decision to have most of its pilots fly at high altitudes above 15.000 feet to avoid anti-aircraft missiles and fire. NATO would appropriately conclude that because of its desire to avoid additional risks to its pilots, it would refrain from attacking certain targets because it could not adequately verify that they were appropriate military targets or take adequate steps to avoid endangering civilians. But it is troubling that some cases NATO has apparently decided to elevate the protection of its pilots over all consideration to the potential harm to civilians." CNN: "To protect its pilots from" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Time for a question, Mr. Ackerman. This is not your chance to give evidence. This is your chance to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I just need to confront him with these, Your Honour, and ask him if that would change his view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the significance of what Human Rights Watch think unless we know who were the experts were who were giving them the advice, what they've assessed, what the appropriate height to bomb from is, on which we've got no factual information at the moment whatsoever. This is just assertion by people who may or may not be qualified to say anything about it. I can't see how it would help the General to answer the question, but possibly you are coming to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about the Army War College, would you consider that a reliable source, General, United States Army War College?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely, it's an authoritative source for the United States armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In an article from the Army War College talking about General Clark and the operation in Kosovo: "He did not mention there was no air force flying against NATO nor that the 15.000-foot limitation was set to ensure there would be no damage to NATO's virtually invulnerable fleet." And then I take it you know that Amnesty International was highly critical of the restriction of 15.000 feet for NATO aircraft. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what's the question, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not a question that's going to help this Trial Chamber. Move on to something that's going to help it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that pilots were restricted to flying above 15.000 feet for a significant amount of the campaign?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had this instruction, that's true, but I think this had no major impact on the accuracy of their bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that was not my question, was it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not your question, but that is the decisive point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this height, Mr. Ackerman, and if it's not related to the failure to accurately target targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll tell you if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would be grateful, because I'm not following the purpose of the cross-examination at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This witness says that it's disproportionate when you're being fired at from a house to fire back with a tank round, but it's not disproportionate to drop a bomb from 15.000 feet when you can't be assured of any accuracy at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it is a question of accuracy, which you've just told me it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It can be a position of accuracy, but my position is it's irresponsible to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What else is it? Does the bomb cause more damage from 15.000 feet than from a lower height? Is that one of the issues or is it purely accuracy? Help me, because I don't know. I don't know anything about this subject until you give me some facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it it's two things. I think it has to do with accuracy and I think it has to do with whether or not you can, as a commander, take actions to protect your troops ahead of, in some cases, concern for safety for civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness told you, yesterday, it was safer from the point of accuracy to bomb from 15.000 feet than low-flying aircraft. Where is the optimum height? Is that what we're going to explore?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, but I think that statement that it's safer to bomb from a higher altitude is absolutely untrue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the answer you got and that's what we'll have to deal with. No doubt you'll bring different evidence to cast different light on it. You're reading comments from other organisations, qualified or unqualified, about flying at 15.000 feet is of no assistance to us in this trial. So please carry on with questions and not submissions and argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, are you aware of a computer programme by the name of BugSplat?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It wasn't used to your knowledge during this campaign?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea which computer programmes they used; that was not my responsibility to look into computer programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know anything about a computer programme that is designed to predict in the targeting process designed to predict collateral damage?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that they had computer programmes, but I'm not aware of the details of such a computer programme. Again, I should say, I am not the one who had to turn the little screws in this campaign. I had to make sure that strategic guidance was properly observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This campaign was carried out in phases, was it not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the first active phase of the campaign, which on paper was the second phase, the first active phase was to establish air superiority over Kosovo and to grade, command, and control across the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How long did it take for you to establish air superiority?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the best of my recollection, Mr. Ackerman, approximately after one week we had achieved it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at what point would you say it was that the Yugoslav air force was unable to operate in that theatre?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Yugoslav air force never made a real attempt to challenge NATO aircraft, so this question has to be answered by someone who was in command of the Yugoslav air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was the Yugoslav air force operating in Kosovo, primarily the jet aircraft that they had available, fighter aircraft, operating in Kosovo after that first week?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that they really made a serious attempt to use fighter aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think you'll agree with me that, you know, once you have in this targeting process gathered all the intelligence that you can and decided that a target is legitimate and tack is justified, that even with all that a mistake can occur and collateral damage can occur; true?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what it was you believed before you carried out the attack may not have been the case. The intelligence may have been faulty and the strength and number of forces may have been incorrect and things of that nature; correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could happen with all intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And in its bombing campaign, NATO suffered from faulty information at times at the expense of civilian lives, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not confirm that. I think we took great pain to make sure that we did not sacrifice any civilian life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about just a few instances where these kind of mistakes I think probably occurred. Do you recall the attack on a civilian passenger train at Grdelica Gorge on 12 April of 1999?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was on attempt, wasn't it, to take out the railway bridge there. And the first bomb inadvertently, after it had been released apparently, the pilot saw the train but it was too late to do anything and the bomb hit a train carrying civilians?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how the pilot described the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ten civilians were killed and 15 were injured, right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I learned as well after the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when the pilot realised there had been a mistake and he had actually hit the train instead of the bridge, instead of pulling off the attack he decided to try again to hit the bridge, dropped another bomb, and hit the train again, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he released two weapons, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I think we can probably agree that you had reliable intelligence information that that railway was being used for military purposes; and if you did, the bridge was a legitimate target?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bridge was considered to be a legitimate target.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in the process of bombing that legitimate military target by mistake, civilians were killed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, Mr. Ackerman. They were unfortunately killed, that's correct, and we examined this event very carefully. We learned that there were a couple of really unfortunate coincidences happened and for that reason regrettably this loss of civilian life occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Another instance was an attack on a convoy, the Djakovica convoy, on 14 April of 1999, in which 70 to 75 civilians were killed and about a hundred injured. And at the time of the attack, NATO believed that this was a military and not a civilian convoy; correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, apparently, three aircraft were involved; an F-16 and two Jaguars operating from 15.000 feet or above. The bombs dropped by the Jaguars both missed their targets, and one of the bombs dropped by the F-16 missed its target. Are you area of that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am not familiar with the details. Again, I have to tell you, it was not my task to look into every single attack. You are simply confusing the responsibilities between strategic oversight and tactical monitoring.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't expect you to answer anything you don't know. And when I asked you yesterday about the ability of a pilot to distinguish a target from 15.000 feet, you said that the capability they had in the cockpit was quite good and that that was not a problem. In this case, the cockpit video made by the pilot, the -- what he could see on his video in his aeroplane, made it look like the vehicles in the convoy were tractors. But when he viewed it with his naked eye, he said they looked more like military vehicles so he went ahead and carried out the attack. And this was at night, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I said this was at night, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I'm sorry. Again, I should say, I was not the air controller. I don't know whether this attack occurred at day or night. It didn't happen for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please understand that it's perfectly okay to just tell me I don't know. I understand that some of these things you probably are not going to know?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned, Mr. Ackerman, you tried to ask me questions of which you don't understand anything, like the difference between low-level flying and high-level altitude attacks. In sharp contrast to you, I've been sitting in aircraft of that type, and I know what the difference is and for that reason I made my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I can only ask you questions, General, based on the things that I learn and the things that I read, and I'm not going to get into an argument with you about that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you told me that I did not tell the truth, and that is something which I simply don't accept, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand you wouldn't accept that. I want to talk to you about the bombing of RTS television station in Belgrade. Ten -- somewhere between ten and 17 civilians were killed in that attack, and you're familiar with that attack, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And NATO claimed that that facility was being used as a radio relay station to support activities of the FRY military and special police forces and, therefore, was a legitimate military target; correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, one of the things that I think is curious about that: If that was the justification, why is it that what was attacked was the ground floor of that building and not the giant transmission tower standing next to it, if you're trying to cut off the transmissions? That makes no sense to me, does it to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, first of all do you know the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the answer to this question, since as I have said again and again, Your Honour, I was not in the targeting process. That was done by the responsible force people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There you have the answer to that, Mr. Ackerman. But even if the General had known the answer to that question, what would have been the relevance? There may be, but I would like you to explain to me the relevance in the in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: An announced justification of attacking it was to cut off communications facilities, when in fact you don't attack the antenna but you attack the ground floor of a building. It's more directed at personnel than it is at the problem they're announcing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. But what is the relevance to the trial about whether these men here are responsible for committing war crimes, which require mens rea and don't require exploration of negligent conduct by them or anyone else. Why are we exploring circumstances of NATO attacks, which you yourself have suggested two were negligent rather than deliberate. We might have reached a deliberate one now according to your proposition, but even then what's the point in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the point is it's difficult to make a difference between what's negligent and what's deliberate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the point in exploring NATO's activity for this trial? This type of activity? There are purposes in exploring NATO conduct and NATO intentions and NATO policy in certain context in this trial but not this stuff, unless you can explain to me what the relevance is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only person I'm trying this case to are you and your colleagues. So if this is not having any impact on you, I'm wasting my time and I will not go forward with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're demonstrating your inability to tell me what the purpose of this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the purpose of it is the contrast between this witness on the one hand saying, You can't sit on a hill with a tank and fire at a building from which you're being fired at, but we can drop bombs from 15.000 feet on civilian targets on the pretext that we're dropping a bomb on a communication facility, when in fact what you're doing is killing civilians and leaving the antenna intact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you see, Mr. Ackerman, that takes us nowhere on the question whether the conduct of the forces with the tanks were acting in a way which was inappropriate and, indeed, deliberate and whether the NATO conduct was a deliberate attempt to cause civilian injury. There doesn't seem to be any direct comparison between the two on the basis on which you've presented the matter. And in any event even if NATO are major war criminals, which I don't know, does it matter in this trial? That's a separate issue. We're not here to judge NATO's activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I understand that. And I'm not suggesting we're here to Judge NATO's activity. But I'm suggesting here that what we are here to do is judge what is appropriate and inappropriate in warfare of this kind, what's an appropriate and inappropriate target, what's excessive and not. And to a great extent, what NATO believes is appropriate and not excessive has a lot to do with what is in fact appropriate and not excessive, I would suggest to you. And we all know that NATO was investigated regarding its behaviour during this NATO bombing campaign and was found that they had not violated international humanitarian law. So the presumption is that the actions NATO took are appropriate actions to take. And if that's the case, then we must compare those with the actions taken by the people sitting behind me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the judgement made by those responsible for that decision is of no significance to us. We will decide this case purely on the evidence. And the evidence that we should concentrate on is the evidence that relates to the guilt or innocence of these accused, and we would be grateful if you would now do that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I would hope the evidence and the law. I would have talked with the witness about the attack on the Chinese Embassy and the attack on Korisa village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would like to go now, General, to some things that General Clark talked about in his book, and we'll get through this fairly briefly. He talks about having discussions with you about possible NATO involvement in Kosovo in early 1998, correct? Like maybe March or April?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was around April, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he says probably April or early May: "I discussed the Kosovo situation frequently with Klaus Naumann and other European military leaders. We could see that NATO's involvement was practically inevitable." Now, how was it as early as April or May of 1998 it seemed to you and General Clark and other military leaders that NATO involvement in Kosovo was inevitable?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what General Clark is saying in his book is his conclusion. He did not say -- sometimes even the ambiguous English language is quite precise. He did not say that we, the other European leaders, agreed with his conclusions. And we saw that the -- we were confronted with a spiral of escalation and counter-escalation, and there was a risk that innocent people could lose their lives in the Kosovo situation. That was the gist of our discussions. But since this is the first time I got the opportunity to respond to you on earlier things, I simply would like to remind you, had you tried to ask me on the Chinese Embassy bombing, you would have missed your point since I was no longer in charge at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad you got to answer a question that I wasn't permitted to ask you. This operation that General Clark says was inevitable, NATO had never carried out such an operation in its history, had it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO had never used its weapons in any other operation before that. If I leave aside the last -- no, it was -- I think it was primarily an American operation, the last minutes of the Bosnia conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Doesn't it -- doesn't it seem strange to you when something unprecedented like that is discussed, that all of a sudden it becomes inevitable?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, Mr. Ackerman, no decision had been reached, no agreement had been reached. We were at the beginning of an involvement of the alliance, and we all knew that the decision to use force will always be a political decision, not a military one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- you could perhaps help us a little more then getting closer to the point here. It seems to me that there is a respectable argument, based on what we heard from you yesterday, that the decision to bomb had actually been taken by the a 19th of January. Now, would you say anything to persuade us to the contrary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the decision had not been taken by the 19th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what I didn't see in yesterday's evidence what it was that happened after the 19th of January that gave rise to that decision, and how it actually emerged. It seems that we leapt over the activity of the International Contact Group, which you said did cause unrest and confusion to the point where we have the final effort by Holbrooke, which collapses and results in an immediate bombing campaign. Now, what is it in there that actually occurs that pushes NATO into engaging in the bombing campaign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in January 1999, the political processes in Rambouillet and Paris started. That was a hope to achieve a peaceful settlement of the Kosovo conflict; that was our sincere hope at the time. When these two political processes collapses, a last effort was made to avoid a military action, and that was to dispatch Mr. Holbrooke to Belgrade. When this also failed, there was no other option left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, the evidence -- there is evidence in the case that the talks collapsed, perhaps because the goal-posts were moved, that preconditions to agreement were changed at a very late stage in the negotiations. Now, that may or may not be the case; there's evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for me it's extremely difficult --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I understand. If you just hear me through. And, therefore, it is arguable that there was justification on the Yugoslav side for agreement not being reached. Now, let's move forward from that. Just leave that hanging as a possibility. What is this last-ditch effort stopping -- what's going on at that moment in reality on the ground that's pushing NATO to the point where it says, We've got to take action? Why was it then necessary, when it hadn't been necessary up until then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we saw the failure of the political processes. At the same time, and in parallel, we saw the deterioration of the situation on the ground. This permanently -- well, the permanent escalation which took place on the ground in form of violence of both sides, I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's the bit that's missing from yesterday's evidence I think. Are you saying that after Rambouillet [Realtime transcript read in error "Avram bu ya"], there was an up surge in violence? Because you told us there was a calm period at the time of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they both were jockeying for political influence by trying to portray themselves as innocent or being victims, there was a little bit of calming down. But then when it became obvious that the processes were about to fail, we saw an increase of violence and we had no instruments to stop it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 17, line 5, you said after Rambouillet, and it says Avram bu ya.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I hope they'll manage to correct that one in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They will now, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On June 16th, 1998, NATO carried out an operation called Determined Falcon. You are familiar with that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell the Judges what that is?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall properly, it was a demonstrative exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How was it operated? How was it carried out?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That you have to ask the commander who carried it out. I was involved in designing the concept for something like this. I think I have stated repeatedly in public that I was not entirely happy with the decision to launch that thing, but I had to follow the political guidance issued by defence ministers in this case. But it -- it was supposed to be a warning signal to the Yugoslav republic not to escalate further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what it was a number of NATO fighter aircraft, combat aircraft that were flown across Albania up to the Serbian border just to let the Serbs know that you had the capabilities to do that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. They never entered Yugoslav air-space.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. Now, in July, after that operation, are you aware of the concern, especially from France and German sources, that NATO should not be threatening or using force without specific authorisation from the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a permanent discussion going on, Mr. Ackerman, in NATO headquarters on the question of legitimacy and legality of the use of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And NATO had never gone even as far as ACTWARN [Realtime transcript read in error "ACTORD"] status before without approval from the Security Council, had it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- we don't -- according to NATO's procedures, nobody needs to have an authority by the United Nations to take steps like activation warning or activation order. The only thing for which, according to the view of the majority of the nations in summer 1998, UN authorisation was necessary was the real application of the use of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the transcript on line 17 says ACTORD and what I said was ACTWARN status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can you tell me again the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The relevance of this is the unique nature of NATO's operation here. It never happened before. This is something new and unique.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the relevance of that to the situation that we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there certainly has been a question about the legality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the relevance of the legality to the situation we are dealing with? See, it's all very interesting and we'd love to explore it if it were appropriate, Mr. Ackerman, but what is the purpose of exploring it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm finished with the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I take it no other counsel have questions if you're continuing with your cross, because we're not far off your suggested time for cross-examination as Defence -- a team of Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wasn't aware. I thought we had until tomorrow at 3.30 if we needed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The guide-line is you have the same time as the Prosecution for live witnesses; and because of the 92 ter, you have another hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe the Prosecution has another witness I don't know about. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Today, I don't know. Does that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you set aside all this time for this week. And I know you've expressed concern about not being able to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you want to go beyond the normal guide-lines, we expect to be told and we expect to do so on relevant material. Just because we have time is no basis for exploring things of no relevance to the trial, and no one has suggested yet that the Defence will require extra time to deal with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think you must know that this is one of the more important witnesses that is being called by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm struggling to see that we're benefitting from this exercise at the moment. I wonder if someone else would have more -- perhaps you would give way to someone else now, Mr. Ackerman, to see if there are more direct issues we can deal with and then come back to you if we have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm nearly finished, Your Honour. And if you will have a little patience, I will finish. And I certainly don't want to do anything that's not useful to you. That's my whole purpose is to try to assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it true, General, that by August it had become clear to General Clark, and probably to you also, that what was necessary in Serbia was regime change, that Milosevic had to go?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was never a conclusion which was discussed at NATO headquarters, and I can tell you that I never had a discussion with General Clark about regime change, which was clearly beyond the portfolio of military people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. There are a couple of maps that I want to show you very quickly and briefly. The first one is 4D88.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I actually gave you courtesy copies of the full-sized map that's hard to look at on the e-court. And I want to give a copy of each of these to the usher to give to the General so he can look at the full maps if he wants to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, when you get these, up in the upper left-hand corner, you'll see the exhibit numbers 4D88 and 4D89.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if we can zoom in a little bit at the lower left-hand corner where the legend is just to begin. I don't know if we can do that or not. Okay. We've got to get.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Down in the lower left-hand corner there is a legend and it shows what the marks on the map consist of. And this is called a mines and KFOR route map, and I don't know whether you've ever seen it before or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I couldn't have seen it since when KFOR started its operations, I was no longer in active military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. I thought you'd seen it since then. But in any event if you look down at the bottom, the legend shows that one symbol shows cluster bomb unit strike sites and the other shows minefields.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And now if we'll zoom out and look at the left side along the Albanian border, just as an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You'll see a number of cluster bomb drop sites. Do you see those?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see them, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at 4D89. And 4D89 is another NATO-KFOR map, and it's essentially the same map. It shows cluster bomb drop sites and mine sites, but it also adds depleted uranium sites and they're in the form of little white triangles.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I doubt whether you're in a position to tell us whether or not that's accurate, actually I'm sure you're not. But because they are maps created apparently by NATO and KFOR, I take it you would at least presume their accuracy?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply cannot answer the question whether these maps are accurate, since as I told you earlier on when KFOR started and these maps had to be produced after KFOR was in the country, I was no longer in military service. I see these maps today for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm finished with those. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if they're being tendered, I have an objection because I'm not sure about the foundation. I see some handwritten it looks like B/C/S on the bottom of the last map. I don't know who put that on there or what that pertains to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll refuse to admit these, because the witness has absolutely no knowledge of the content of these. If they have to come in, they'll have to come in through a witness who can say something relevant about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In mid-September, General, of 1998, are you aware of Mr. Clark's trip to -- General Clark's trip to Washington and his meeting with Secretary of Defence Cowen where he said to the secretary, Things need to move forward. We're running out of time to save NATO and our credibility?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I'm not aware of General Clark's statement to his defence minister. He also, as you may know, had a double-headed function in his command capacity. He was on the one hand NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, and on the other hand he had an American command responsibility as the Commander-in-Chief US EUCOM. In which capacity he travelled to Washington, I don't know. And I can only tell you that he never made a statement like this in the NATO Council, which is the appropriate body for taking decisions at NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In a meeting of the NATO defence ministers on September 23rd in Vilamoura in Portugal, I assume you were at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General Clark says that Javier Solana said there that he determined to save NATO's reputation in the region and its credibility. Do you remember that statement by Solana?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that statement by Secretary-General Solana, and I don't believe that he made a statement like this in the NATO Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In Exhibit P720, which is a paper written by you, I think the title of it is: "There Will Be Another Conflict," you say on page 4 of that paper: "If NATO had not acted, the credibility of the alliance would have suffered irreparable damage." Now, you can't deny that one, can you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I can't. I remember that one. But this is a totally different context, and it was written after the Kosovo air campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Transcript says you said you can't remember it. You remember it, don't you? You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It says "of course, I can't." I think there should be a period, then it says "I can remember that one."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can remember, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, what I'm suggesting to you is that at least by September, there was concern being expressed by Clark and Solana and perhaps you that failing to go forward with the bombing campaign was going to affect NATO's credibility. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- the question of credibility arose again and again, Mr. Ackerman. You should never forget, NATO started to -- to influence the Kosovo situation, and it issued warnings. It stated threats to use force beginning in April 1998, then, nevertheless, the situation escalated. And there was, indeed, a discussion of credibility whether the alliance had any chance at all to influence the situation and to achieve a peaceful solution of it. So the question of credibility was a serious matter. But I should also add having followed the discussions in the NATO Council more or less day by day throughout this period, the credibility alone would never have been accepted as a reason to go to the use of force by the 16 NATO nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, yesterday, you talked a little bit about the meetings between Holbrooke and Milosevic on the 12th and 13th of November, and that Holbrooke then came back to Brussels and reported to NATO that he had entered into this agreement with Milosevic. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's the case, isn't it, that that was a very distressing piece of news to NATO? NATO didn't want to hear that a settlement had been reached by Holbrooke and Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an allegation which is your allegation. I cannot confirm that. I can only tell you that I had never seen anything else but the desire of NATO to find a solution without using force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, my only source is General Clark on this issue. General Clark says that when Solana learned about this, he said to General Clark: "This won't work. It means that NATO will have no role. This is terrible. You must fix this." That was Solana's reaction to the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement. Aren't you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you, Mr. Ackerman, that perhaps General Clark wrote it in that way, but I can't deny. But I can tell you that Solana never stated something like this in the NATO Council and never stated something like this in the discussions which he and I had, and after all I was his top military advisor. What we saw when Holbrooke came back was that one advantage was tied to Holbrooke's result and that was that the Kosovo conflict began to be internationalised, and that was a major political achievement. So I think Clark may have written this based on his recollections, but it doesn't properly reflect what Solana thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Clark puts a quote in his book as to what Solana told him. "This won't work, and it means that NATO will have no role. This is terrible. You must fix this." Now, you told us, yesterday, about some distress that you had because during the whole Rambouillet process, NATO was out of the loop and not involved. Now, isn't it the case that it was NATO's position at this point that the OSCE verification process was a horrible mistake, that it wouldn't work, that it put NATO out of the loop, and needed to be undermined? Wasn't that the NATO position at that point?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, this was not the NATO's position. That is your conclusion, and I cannot confirm that something like this has ever been the conclusion at which the NATO Council arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you and Holbrooke -- when you and Clark went off to Belgrade to negotiate terms after Holbrooke and Milosevic had arrived at their agreement, isn't it the case that at least Clark went there with the directions from Solana that he must fix this horrible situation, and isn't that why those negotiations were put in such a way that it was almost impossible for the Serbs to give up to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the form of the question. It's compound, and it also I think inaccurately states what this witness has said about what Solana and Clark may have discussed. He doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This question, Mr. Hannis, is about the trip, I assume, on the 19th of January -- oh, no. This is the 24th and 25th of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. It's right after Clark indicates that he was instructed by Solana to fix this situation, it won't work because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's ask the question in stages, Mr. Ackerman. What's the first question you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After that situation had developed where it became clear that Holbrooke and Milosevic had an agreement, you and Clark were sent off to Belgrade to negotiate some of the agreements, to implement that agreement, right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, we were not sent to Belgrade to fix something. We were sent to Belgrade to make clear, as I stated yesterday, to Mr. Milosevic that he had to withdraw forces, police and military forces, which were in excess to peacetime strength and to end hostilities there. That was our task. And if you kindly would look into what Mr. Holbrooke discussed with Mr. Milosevic or perhaps ask the -- the person sitting behind you what the contents of these talks were, you will presumably arrive at the same conclusion as Clark and I did at the time; namely, that the question of withdrawal of additional forces had not been discussed between Milosevic and Holbrooke in a way which would have contributed to the end of hostilities. That was our task. We had to, so to say, fill a gap which was left over in the Holbrooke-Milosevic talks, and we were not sent by the NATO Council to Belgrade, as you suggested, to fix something and to bring NATO back into the game.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You say it was not to bring NATO back into the game?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the political objective. The objective was to get the forces out and to end hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to go to a completely different subject now. And I just want to ask you before I ask you any questions about it, do you have knowledge about the surveillance capabilities of NATO during the actual bombing campaign; the drones and the satellites and all of the capability to surveil the ground in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen the results, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: NATO had at its disposal fairly significant air assets, including A-10 Warthogs, which are designed to destroy tanks; correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but they have nothing to do with surveillance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know they have absolutely nothing to do with surveillance, and I didn't ask you if they did. What you had for surveillance was Predator drones and there was some German drones, some French drones, I think maybe another one or two kinds -- maybe four or five kinds of drones that were being used as surveillance at that time, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And also, there was satellite capability, satellite imagery?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And was it true that that imagery enables you to pretty thoroughly observe the movements of VJ assets, especially heavy weaponry tanks, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under fair weather conditions, almost perfectly well; under adverse weather conditions, there was worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The drones could fly under the cloud cover on occasion, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the drones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you were able to find a tank or artillery moving around, then you could bring in the A-10s and take them out?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically, yes; again, depending to some extent on weather conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that in the entire NATO bombing campaign that you believed that the death of only 500 civilians was a -- a fairly minimal number and an acceptable number, although even one may be too many at times. Is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did never say that 500 civilian casualties were acceptable. I said I think -- if I repeated -- if I recall it properly, I said these were 500 too many.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. But not an indication, I think you told us -- I haven't got the transcript in front of me. I think you told us that that wasn't an indication of overreaching on NATO's part at least.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you think of a bombing campaign which lasts for 70 days, using some X thousand of ammunitions and then you have 1 percent more or less of the ammunition hitting the wrong targets producing collateral damage, you cannot talk of an inaccurate campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if it's the case that during that bombing campaign you actually killed a little over a thousand members of the Yugoslav armed forces, then would you say that a ratio of 2:1 armed forces:civilians is an acceptable ratio?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that this is acceptable, if I have said earlier on that 500 killed civilians are 500 too many. I'm missing the logic of your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So am I, and I think we have all that we are prepared to allow from you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have one last question and then I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's hope it's got some relevance to the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you expressed a concern during your testimony in Milosevic that the actions of NATO may have been a bit precipitous when you said this, and I think this is page 6996: "I think if you were in such a conflict, you should presumably talk to both sides and try to influence them to the best and the best possible way. Perhaps we could have. We could have reduced difficulties in this area. Whether it would have led to a peaceful solution, I cannot tell you, Your Honour, but I live with the conviction one should make every attempt possible to defuse a situation before one uses military force to enforce peace." And I take it you still accept that statement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Naumann. My name is Djuro Cepic, attorney-at-law, and I will have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] -- language to reply on that language, so I will ask you in B/C/S. [Interpretation] Mr. Naumann, during your yesterday's testimony, you answered a question put by His Honour, Judge Bonomy, pertaining your report submitted to NATO pertaining to the meeting of the 19th of January, 1999, and the notes were mentioned pertaining to the same meeting. There was a mention of Podujevo and ethnic cleansing at a number of pages. And at page 39 of the transcript, you stated that the ethnic cleansing was conducted by the Serbs. Do you still stand by that assertion, Mr. Naumann?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the impression we gained at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You were not in Kosovo in that time, were you, Mr. Naumann?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You received your information from the Kosovo Verification Mission, that is from the OSCE mission. Is that correct, Mr. Naumann?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated yesterday that we received the information from the OSCE mission, from the remnants of the KDOM mission, and of course from intelligence which we gained.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, before this Bench, some high officials of the Kosovo Verification Mission appeared, and they were in the field at the time and they participated in the resolution of the crisis which ensued concerning Podujevo. And Mr. Ciaglinski was even honoured by the UK for his participation in the mission. Everything points to the fact that within the given period, the ethnic cleansing at Podujevo was carried out by the KLA and that all Serbs and other non-Albanians were driven out from the villages you specified. Therefore, everything you said is correct, apart from the fact that the ethnic cleansing was conducted by the Serbs, rather, it was done by the so-called KLA. Everything I've said so far, would any of it change your position on the matter?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the people who were on the ground gave you the evidence which you just described, I am not in a position to say that they are not telling the truth. The only thing that I could tell you was the information which I got at the time at NATO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Naumann.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the basis was Mr. Ciaglinski's evidence, first of all, as well as some other witnesses who testified on it, and I have in mind General Drewienkiewicz and General Loncar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, at the meeting of the 15th of October, 1998, General Perisic was present as well, as you stated. Inter alia, there were requests made to withdraw part of the VJ units, specifically the 211th Armoured Brigade was mentioned. My question is: Did you know that pursuant to General Perisic's orders on the 16th that unit was withdrawn, and all the other units pursuant to your request were withdrawn and it was done during that day?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always had the impression and the discussion, Mr. Cepic, that General Perisic really tried to keep the VJ out of this emerging conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Naumann. Mr. Perisic also participated in the agreement, and I believe you met him subsequently on the 25th of October, 1998. It was defined that the units were to return to their garrisons, apart from three or four companies which were used to protect certain roads, as well as the border units which were to stay to secure the state border. As opposed to the special agreement which defined the exact number of the police, this agreement, as well as some other agreements, did not define any exact figure of military personnel. Isn't that correct, Mr. Naumann?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the agreement is in front of the Court, and I can only repeat what I have said also in the Milosevic case, that the Serb side honoured their agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Naumann. We've touched upon another question, that is to say winter exercises. Mr. Naumann, do you perhaps know that all exercises carried out by the Army of Yugoslavia took place outside barracks. All unit movements were monitored by the Kosovo Verification Mission. And as for planned training that took place outside barracks of the Army of Yugoslavia, the Army of Yugoslavia actually provided documents to the Kosovo Verification Mission, that is to say provided documents to the OSCE about this. Do you know about that, Mr. Naumann?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that it provided information in great detail to the Kosovo Verification Mission. That exercises are carried out outside the barracks is normal proceedings, and I think that in -- we are talking presumably about the January/February 1999 time-frame. At this time, according to my recollection, the VJ cooperated relatively smoothly with the Kosovo -- with the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Naumann. Now that we're on the subject of exercises, I would like to ask you for your own assessment. A tank column of only a few tanks is on the move along a road on which it had been carrying exercises for the past 20 or 30 years. This is an exercise for training young recruits, young soldiers. This is something that the Kosovo Verification Mission had been informed upon; however, this column is fired at. The column is being targeted by hand-held rocket-launchers, and burst ones at that. One tank is damaged, three soldiers are injured. The army responds to this attack from its own tanks. Is that a legitimate response, Mr. Naumann?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as I understood your CV, you have considerable artillery experience, too. If a battery of the so-called KLA targets the positions of the army with 120-millimetre mortars, is it legitimate to respond with artillery against those positions from which the firing had taken place?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without any doubt, and this would be covered by what we said in the last paragraph of the statement which we signed with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Naumann. Judge Bonomy, the Honourable Presiding Judge, asked you yesterday about the name of the village that had been shelled, and you mentioned that in the context of your arrival at the meeting on the 24th of October, 1998. And you did not know the name of that village. I made a considerable effort trying to find in the documentation of the Kosovo Verification Mission and of KDOM and of the Serb side what the name of this village is, or at least of the region, but I didn't manage to find it. I didn't manage to find a single bit of information about a single village being shelled in that period. Do you allow for the possibility that you were perhaps misinformed, Mr. Naumann?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only thing, Mr. Cepic, I can tell you about this is that I got this piece of information on the flight to Belgrade from the NATO intelligence division. I do not know which source they had, but I trust if they really make the effort to inform me on the flight that they had a solid piece of information, otherwise they wouldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Naumann. You mentioned the presence of Shaun Byrnes at one of the meetings you had in Belgrade. As you know, he was the representative of KDOM, the American department. Just one question: Do you perhaps know whether Mr. Byrnes, in these talks and later, informed you about all the verifications carried out by KDOM. There were 30 of them that took place without any objections and in the best possible order. This is the verification of anti-aircraft systems of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Mr. Byrnes informed us about what he is doing with the KDOM mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Naumann, since you held one of the most important positions in the NATO alliance, are you aware of the exact number of members of NATO forces who were deployed during the spring in Albania and Macedonia while NATO was operating in Kosovo, Serbia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; NATO air force, that is?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO air forces were not deployed in Macedonia and in Albania at the time. We had some -- we had some NATO ground forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me. [Interpretation] I think this is a mistake. I am asking about ground forces, the number of ground troops in Macedonia and Albania.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. We had a relatively small component in Macedonia, which was a part of the -- well, the team which was there to act in case that the Kosovo Verification Mission should come under attack. It was very limited in number. I don't -- I don't remember the precise figures. I knew it at the time, but you may forgive me now with eight years' distance I do not remember the precise figures. But it was approximately brigade sized, I think. And in Albania, we had also a couple of forces, but they were there to help the UNHCR to establish refugee camps. So they were really there for humanitarian purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now that we're on the subject of Albania and the NATO presence in Albania, General Clark in his book stated that there was an operations group in Albania in order to support KLA forces. Are you aware of the existence of such a group that was supporting KLA?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you, Mr. Cepic, that NATO never authorised anyone to support the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Naumann. As for the personnel levels of the ground forces in Macedonia and Albania, as the operation of NATO forces started, it went up, didn't it, the personnel levels?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be that the levels increased a little bit, but it was not significant. And this increase, I think, was to some extent a response to the influx of refugees which took place also in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, in this courtroom we heard about certain fighting and actions that took place along the border between Albania and Kosmat. You should know about the use of strategic bombers, B-52 during the month of May 1999 in the Pastrik area in support of ground forces of the KLA in order to penetrate the border. General Clark wrote about that as well.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends very much which time in May you refer to, Mr. Cepic. May I remind you that I left my job on the 6th of May, 1999. So when B-52 attacks two places after that time, I may have read about it in the press at that time but I was no longer in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Naumann.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could I please just have a moment to look at my notes to see whether I have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, yesterday you said that you took part in planning the targeting of the police building in Belgrade. It is a generally-known fact that this building you talked about and that was hit was an administrative building of the Ministry of the Interior and that it had been fully vacated before the NATO bombing started. Could you tell me what the reason was to bomb an empty administrative building in the immediate vicinity of the biggest hospital in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. That's compound and he hasn't established from this witness whether or not he knew it was empty, if indeed it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think what I've learned in listening to this cross-examination is that Mr. Naumann is perfectly able to deal with compound questions. And, indeed, when we try to break them down for him, he insists on answering the compound question. So we'll let him deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I had no information, Mr. Cepic, that the building was vacant. We were -- when we talked about this, we were told that this was a headquarters of the police and a building of the Ministry of the Interior. The evacuation of the building was not mentioned. And whether it really was used as a headquarters of the police, whether it's administrative or not, I would regard it as a legitimate target. And what I did, I stated yesterday, and I'm glad that you just confirmed that the hospital was there. And, obviously, despite the fact that I think some six cruise missiles went into the building, no collateral damage occurred to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, there was great damage. All the glass paneling had been broken. The patients were considerably disturbed. A few hundred metres away the General Staff headquarters had been hit, and that was a building that was empty, too. A few civilians who were near that building got killed. Are you aware of that, Mr. Naumann?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any killings of civilians, and I was -- having listened to quite a lot of broadcasts of more or less based on Tanjug reporting, I would be really surprised if they hadn't mentioned the killing of civilians with -- in their daily news casts -- news reports where they anyway enjoyed that considerable advantage over NATO since they reported in the morning at 6.00, where we weren't allowed to state anything until 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, what would you say to this; if many reports about this had been broadcast on television - there is numerous evidence on this - would you change your position concerning your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, to the best of my knowledge, I have not heard anything about the incident which you just mentioned that civilians were killed when the building of the General Staff was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Naumann. Thank you, Mr. Naumann.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more questions, Your Honours, by your leave. My last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, do you know about the proportion of forces, or rather, the balance of forces between NATO forces and Serbian forces at the time of the action that you took on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the overall balance?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, that NATO was superior to the Serb armed forces, that is something I think which need not be mentioned. Mr. Milosevic himself said that he was pretty well aware that NATO could easily defeat Yugoslavia militarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What would you say to me if I were to give you the ratio of 600:1? This is an assertion made by analysts from American and France.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- I would accept it. It is not -- that's not an issue which I think is important for the proceedings in this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Naumann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Naumann. I would like to put a few questions to you that are somewhat different from the other ones. My first question is as follows. I don't know whether you have your statement, or rather, the first question has to do with your testimony during the Milosevic case. The page reference is 77 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the exact page reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that the KLA did --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, the interpreter didn't catch the page number. Could we have the page number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat it. No problem whatsoever. 7074, lines 1, or rather, 9 to 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You were asked and you said that you noticed that the KLA was being supplied with weapons from abroad. And you said that you proposed a few measures that the NATO Council was supposed to consider, but that you were not given approval to take measure to stop the influx of weapons, which is where it all started from, and that is to say where money was being collected to purchase these weapons. I quoted your statement, and I assume that you stand by it. So my question is as follows: Do you have any knowledge about the money that was collected for the purchase of weapons, that this took place in the countries of western Europe and the United States of America?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object on grounds of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's plain that issues relating to the supply of weapons to the KLA could be relevant. I take the point -- the rather narrow point you make about the strict relevancy of that particular question. But I think the line is relevant and we're not inclined to interfere with Mr. Fila proceeding in this way. I doubt if the source of the weapons is terribly important unless it has something to do with the inability to cut off the source, and that may be the case. So let's hear what you have to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is one matter. Another is testimony given by a witness, before, who complained why Mr. Sainovic was saying why western countries wouldn't stop providing money for the purchase of weapons. If Mr. Hannis remembers what Drewienkiewicz said that would be it, so that is why I am putting the question. So there are two reason, you see?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, do you have any knowledge about the collection of money in western countries for weapons supplies? And my second question is: Why did you not get approval to stop that or prevent it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we discussed the issue of arms smuggling and weapons supply, we had a presentation in NATO headquarters on what was going on, and part of this information was also that money was collected. So I fully stick to what I stated in the Milosevic case. The number two of your question -- well, part two of your question was, Mr. Fila, why we were not given the authority to do something about it. Well, there is one point which I think is in the meantime obvious -- obvious knowledge and general knowledge for everyone. There is one nation in NATO who believes that all steps which are not military nature cannot be actions taken by NATO. This is definitely an outdated point of view, since you cannot cope with today's dangers and risks by simply limiting your activities on military aspects. But this one nation is rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- reluctant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which nation is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I have to answer? It's a violation of NATO's rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, sorry. I would not have asked that unless you said it's obvious knowledge and general knowledge for everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not general knowledge for me, I have to tell you, and if you want me to know you have to tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, I will respond. It's France which is permanently blocking anything which is not military in NATO -- in nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During the meetings that you had, did anyone from the Yugoslav authorities, at any of the meetings, the three that you mentioned and others, did anyone complain about that to you? Did anyone ask you from the side of the Yugoslav authorities to stop this flow of money for the purchase of weapons? For example, Mr. Sainovic, since you mentioned him and he's sitting here.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure, at least I do not recall that anyone mentioned precisely the flow of money or something like this. There was -- and I think it was -- it was Mr. Sainovic who repeatedly stated that there was an outside support to the KLA insurgents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That has exhausted the subject. Our time is a bit limited, so I'll try to move faster. And it's going to be easier for you as a soldier as well. Another thing that I would like to draw your attention to is paragraph 46 in your statement. If you found it, let us go on.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that you stand by what is written here, right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, my question reads as follows: What is your source of information? What is the source of information that led you to conclude that this centre for the coordination of forces was in Nis and then in Belgrade, as you said here? This is an oversimplification, and may I tell you straight away that my military knowledge is zilch. I reached the level of corporal and that was it in the army?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are much better off, Mr. Fila, than my son. He only made it to private first class in the navy, but that doesn't matter. Now, the source of this statement which I made was what the agreed intelligence at NATO headquarters in the days of the Kosovo air campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So this was centralised control over the army and police in operations in Kosovo, that that had to be in Nis and Belgrade, not lower down, right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came to this conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to focus on my client, Mr. Sainovic. Mr. Naumann, when you came to Belgrade, at the first meeting Sainovic was not there - that was our understanding - and at the second meeting on the 24th and 25th of October he was there. Mr. Milosevic introduced him and said he was in charge of Kosovo, whatever his formulation was at the time. Now I would like the usher to show you Defence Exhibit 2D8 in English, of course, because the Serbian version won't mean much to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
