utterances.text: While we're waiting for this document, you know that the agreement between the FRY and the OSCE was actually concluded between those two meetings sometimes around the 16th of October. You were there on the 15th and this took place on the 16, is that right? If you still remember that.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, when you see this document, you will see that this is a decision of the Government of Yugoslavia in relation to cooperation with the OSCE mission in Kosovo. Now, I would like you to look at this document. Please look at paragraph 3 of the document. You can see from paragraph 3 that Mr. Sainovic was Deputy Prime Minister in the Federal Government and that he was appointed President of the Commission for Cooperation with the OSCE. Do you agree -- is that what you see there? And now could I have a look at page 2 of this document. Do you agree with me that that is what is written in this document? Do you actually see it yourself?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, on page 2, you will see that it says Zivadin Jovanovic, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, is the Deputy of the President of the Commission, that's Sainovic. And this decision was signed by the Government of Yugoslavia. It was signed by the Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, Momir Bulatovic. Have you seen this document, or rather, did you see it earlier on? I guess you have seen it before?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm showing this to you for one simple reason. I want to show you the reason, if you agree with me that Milosevic introduced Mr. Sainovic to you the way he did, is because of this appointment that you can see that he is really in charge of cooperation with the OSCE in Kosovo. Was that Mr. Milosevic's wording, or can you simply not remember after eight years? I can barely remember what happened eight days ago, but never mind that. Eight years later, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Mr. Fila, Mr. Milosevic introduced Mr. Sainovic as Vice-president of Serbia and as being responsible for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [In English] Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yugoslavia, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this look like the document specifying his duties in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's pretty similar, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's time for a break, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I will continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help me with the likely length of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some ten minutes, but certainly you can interrupt me as soon as you find my questions to be irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I've got about 34 questions, so under 30 minutes I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan. All right. In that case we'll break for half an hour, so we'll be resuming at 11.00. Could you leave with the usher again, Mr. Naumann, and we'll see you at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, at the meeting on the 24th and the 25th, because it is difficult to separate exactly what happened on which day so I suggest we treat it as a single meeting, you mentioned there was some talk of the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement. You also spoke about the presence of Mr. Durkee, and that there was a mention of one of the preconditions for the Kosovo problem solution is to achieve the balance of the two ethnic groups. As far as I understand, you didn't see the actual agreement, the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see the actual agreement. No, I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I wanted to show that agreement to you. It is Exhibit 2D12. It's a communique by the Serbian government pertaining to the document we've been discussing. It is item 16. Could you please focus on item 4. It says: "The solution has to be based," item 4 within that paragraph. "The solution has to be based on the full respect of equality of all citizens and national communities in Kosovo and Metohija. Full affirmation and equal treatment of their national, confessional, cultural values, and historic patrimony should be guaranteed." Can we please move on to item 8 now. It is stated that: "Members of the national communities shall have additional rights, in order to preserve and express their national, cultural, religious, and linguistic identities in accordance with international standards and the Helsinki Final Act. The national communities shall be legally equal and shall not use their additional rights so as to endanger the rights of other national communities or other rights of citizens." I wanted to show you this so as to be able to ask you a question. The spirit of the talks on the 24th and the 25th of October, among the members of the delegation, specifically Mr. Sainovic, whom I represent, was along the lines of trying to find a solution in order to achieve this. Of course we are discussing Kosovo, and all that is pertaining to the mention of the two ethnic groups. At least those who followed it in the papers who were not members of the government were under the impression that the wish on the part of the Serbian government while you were there on the 24th and the 25th. And otherwise was that a part of their political programme was to find a peaceful solution for Kosovo by establishing equal rights for all ethnic communities, irrespective of their size, and I believe it also had to do with the discussions of the contact group.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question now?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that the spirit of the talks? Was it also along the lines of how Mr. Sainovic addressed you? When he spoke, did he mention the peaceful solution?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, my recollection is slightly different. I do not want to accuse anyone, but I do not have the impression that the spirit of the lines, which you just showed me on this communique, was the governing spirit at the meeting on which we had on the 24th and the 25th of October, 1998. I had the impression -- to say it quite sincerely and openly, I had the impression that the Yugoslav side failed to be wounded, to be attacked, that injustice was done to them, and that they had to respond to defend the sovereignty of their state. And they saw that their actions were legitimate, that they were right to do so as they did. And they wanted to preserve as much as they could of, I should say, Yugoslav influence in the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I agree. But we have a separate Balkan slang, just like you have your jargon in the military. But, for example, you come from Germany where there is a single nation. There are various ethnic groups in our part of the world, at least a dozen in Kosovo alone. That's why this notion of ethnic communities or ethnic groups bears a somewhat different meaning. And I was trying to get to that, but I guess you come from a different background. I am going to continue. In your first statement, that is the notes from 2002, you stated that at that meeting Sainovic, as you put it, participated only in technical discussions. It is in your statement. I don't know whether you recall that. If you don't, I will try and locate it in the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe it's the last sentence in paragraph 26, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He only participated in technical discussions. That is the last sentence of paragraph 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It said he had some involvement in technical discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you still abide by that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Concerning the meeting in January in your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no answer to that question either I think given or recorded. Did you answer it, Mr. Naumann?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I answered, and I said yes. I still believe this para 26 reflects what I took with me as an impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which is rather different from the version of the paragraph that Mr. Fila actually gave you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He had some involvement in the technical discussions. You confirmed that indeed it was as stated in paragraph 26, its last sentence?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 29 of the same document, you state that Milosevic or Sainovic stated in one of the meetings, either on the 24th or the 25th, that if they did not solve the Albanian problem now, the Yugoslavs would have the same problem in 20 years because the Albanians repopulated at a far greater rate. First of all, do you know that their birth rate is the highest in Europe. It was at that time as it is today. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And there was much discussion about whether it was just Milosevic or just Sainovic or both of them, and you were examined about that on a few occasions, even in the Milosevic trial. I wanted to ask you this: Was your recollection better in 2002 when you were undecided as to who said what than today, eight years ago? Are you still uncertain who spoke, who of the two?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I think I'm still uncertain. To the best of my recollection, I do not know precisely who said it. I know there was a discussion about the -- the ethnic relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I wanted to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When the discussion took place, do you know whether both Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Sainovic were present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think at this occasion they both were present. It was in the full plenary meeting I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you are uncertain which of the two said that and you're not certain of it today?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could we please have the reply noted in the transcript, it was yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's noted, Mr. Fila, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am approaching the end of my examination. You mentioned the story Milosevic told you about Drenica. It was mentioned a few times. I want to know something else. Did you feel the need, after you met Milosevic for the last time at the trial, to really do some research, to gain some insight as to what really happened in Drenica. If you recall, he said what we were taught in our history lessons as well, that there was a show-down between the Partisans and the so-called Balisti or the Bali Komentar [phoen] Organisation. And we were taught that they were supported by the fascist Germany. They were trained, financed, and equipped by the Germans. They were a symbol of fascism there, and the Balistas had pretty much the same meaning to us as the expression mentioned to you yesterday and in the meaning it had to the Germans. Did you ever try and find out what indeed happened back in 1946 there?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I listened with great interest what Mr. Milosevic stated in the proceedings then. I tried to get hold of some applications in German language to learn a little more about the history in the Balkans, but I didn't succeed in finding sufficient, clear evidence in -- written in German language. And, unfortunately, I'm not able to read Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you didn't attend the same class as I did. Thank you, this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir, my name is Dan Ivetic and, today, I have some questions for you on behalf of Sreten Lukic. Now, first of all, General, when NATO gave you 48 hours in October of 1998 to go to Belgrade and to try and obtain a last-minute agreement with the Serb side, am I correct that you had pretty good intel or intelligence at that time as to military units and formations, but that you lacked such solid intelligence for the number of police units and personnel?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And am I further correct that during this particular series of meetings and negotiations in Belgrade in October 1998, were you and other NATO personnel and KDOM officials met with Serb and Yugoslav authorities that at that time a very comprehensive written document produced by the Serbian MUP relating to the number of police personnel and police stations in Kosovo and Metohija was provided to both the NATO officials and the KDOM officials?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that such a document was provided, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And based upon that information that was provided by the Serbian MUP, am I correct that it was agreed by all the sides to the negotiations that the "peacetime 1998 base-line level for the police was to be around 10.000, precisely 10.021 personnel in Kosovo and Metohija." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct, Mr. Ivetic, that we accepted 10.000 -- I do not -- don't name it down to 21 or 46; somewhere a little above 10.000 was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, that's fine. And then immediately after the conclusion of these agreements, the Serbian MUP withdrew the excess police units from Kosovo and Metohija and brought themselves within compliance of this number, whether it was 10.000 or 10.021 or 10.045?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the impression that they really withdrew the additional personnel and that they tried to comply with the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to verify the withdrawal of police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. You can -- you described some of the discussions undertaken with various personnel as part of these negotiations at paragraph 16 of your -- it's not a statement, but the summary of the -- of your proofing notes. And at that paragraph, you talk about how General Djordjevic, who did most of the talking, outlined a concern about reducing the police forces because of the threat posed by terrorists. Now, the question I want to ask you is: At that time, did NATO have intel or intelligence about the activities of the KLA and how the KLA was going to react as a result of these October accords and the reduction of Serb forces in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when we negotiated this agreement, Mr. Ivetic, we did of course not have any intelligence on how the KLA might react after an agreement. We had intelligence on the activities of both sides before we started to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And focus --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just to clarify something in my mind own at the moment. Was Mr. Lukic present at any of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. To the best of my knowledge, Your Honour, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The only two of the accused here that you remember seeing are Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic. But you should also understand our situation. We were confronted with a -- with quite a huge crowd. And so you may forgive me, I don't remember the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suppose they would have featured if they had.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And some of them, Your Honour, were wearing a uniform, as I did. And it is a common -- I think really common knowledge that people look different wearing uniform or civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Same thing for robes, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, at the time of the negotiations, let's focus on the KLA. You said that you did have intel about what the various parties were doing leading up to the negotiations. With respect to the KLA, did NATO have intelligence confirming that the KLA was constantly active or increasing their operations at that time leading up to the October 1998 meetings?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- Mr. Ivetic, the information we had or the general assessment at which we had arrived was that the KLA had - if I should say it in my ex-military parlance - had suffered a defeat in summer 1998 and was about to re-organise, re-group. It didn't seem to be too impressive in its capability at this time, but they were re-building their capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And after the agreements were reached in October 1998 and after the Yugoslavs withdrew their forces from Kosovo-Metohija and began implementing the agreement, it was only then that the OSCE-KVM came to the ground to monitor compliance of the parties. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, the OVM -- the KVM, yes. Before that, as you -- as we have discussed repeatedly in these proceedings, the KDOM was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: KDOM. And am I correct that NATO on its part and the KDOM on its part fully cooperated with the KVM and provided to the KVM all the information and documents received from the Serb side, particularly with respect to the base-line of the 10.000 or so police personnel that were permitted in Kosovo-Metohija?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think from -- from our side, from NATO's side, I can confirm to you that NATO provided all the relevant information to the OSCE, and I suspect that the OSCE and KDOM cooperated smoothly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, at paragraph 35 of your -- again, I call it a statement, but it's the -- we agree that it's the notes taken from the proofing session that you had, so it's technically not a statement. But at paragraph 35, you indicate that the Yugoslavs had at least 500 excess police, most of whom were coming from MUP detachments outside of Kosovo. Now, first of all, when you say "500 excess," are we talking about 500 more than this 10.000 give or take?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to the number of this 500-excess police, where exactly had you gotten this information? Was it perhaps from the OSCE-KVM that was on the ground at the time?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, Mr. Ivetic, I should say when -- when we stated -- or when I or Clark stated something as NATO intelligence, we did in most cases not have the precise source. So I think it was a compilation of various informations provided by OSCE, by KDOM, and other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The reason I ask, sir, is that we had testimony from General Drewienkiewicz or DZ, who was the Deputy Head of Mission for the KVM, who testified the other week that in fact he claimed that the KVM did not have access to information relating to the base-line of the police forces; and that in fact he told me at page 21, I believe, lines -- lines 4 through 16, approximately, he seemed to indicate that the first time he had heard any reference of a number of approximately 10.000 policemen was this year, in 2006, when I presented the number to him. How would you react to that? Is there any possibility that he's correct in that assertion?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic, we went with this piece of information to Belgrade on the 19th of January, 1999, and we believed I think that we were given the correct figures based on intelligence sources. But as I told you, I do not know which sources they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you go on to say in that section of your -- of the exhibit that I've been referring to, that special police forces were deployed in Kosovo, which was not acceptable. Now, I presume you're talking about the PJP and the SAJ units of the MUP. I want to ask you, sir, are you aware of the fact that there are detachments of these units which are indigenous to Kosovo and Metohija, that is to say that the Kosovo secretariats of police have their own PJP detachments from their own personnel and that the SAJ actually has a detachment that has always been permanently based in Kosovo? Were you aware of that at the time that you made your statement that special police forces were deployed in Kosovo, which was not acceptable?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware that there were so to say indigenous special police elements in Kosovo. But when we stated this in January 1999, the intelligence we had in our hands was that there had been forces poured into Kosovo which were not based in Kosovo but had been brought in from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 17 of this statement, you describe -- you begin talking about Malisevo, a village within Kosovo-Metohija. Do you remember why Malisevo and that entire region surrounding that town was important, and why it featured so much in the negotiations to the point where even the Byrnes-Djordjevic agreement specifically deals with that particular area of Kosovo-Metohija?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we went to Belgrade, Mr. Ivetic, I was not aware of the centrality of Malisevo for both sides. And I learned in the proceedings that at this place, obviously, a KLA headquarters had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And had you also hear or learn that Malisevo had been one of the bases from which arms and munitions had been smuggled in across the border?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was mentioned in these talks that we had in this night, 24 to 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And was KDOM, the US-KDOM mission, was it eager to address Malisevo and retain a reduction of the police forces situated there?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that KDOM had more or less drawn our attention to the centrality of Malisevo before we started the talks. So to Clark and me, this -- this insistence on Malisevo came a little bit as a surprise I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I presume that since it came as a surprise to you, your knowledge of the KLA presence in Malisevo, that came -- that would have come from KDOM as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well -- and most of the information we had came from KDOM.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did it appear to you, sir, that KDOM was feeling pressure from the KLA to obtain a reduction of the police force in Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the impression that KDOM -- the only one I talked to was Shaun Byrnes, that he was under pressure from the side of the KLA. I had the impression that Byrnes was a rather, I should say, impartial player.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And based upon the knowledge that you have -- that you obtained from Mr. Byrnes relating to Malisevo during these discussions, would -- would you say that due to the concerns over the presence of a KLA base and the smuggling of KLA weapons into Malisevo, that in fact the Serbs would have a legitimate concern and a justified reason for maintaining a police presence in that area?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we -- if you look at the general gist of the 25th October agreement, we acknowledged the principle that the Serbian police should execute its rights in a lawful and proportionate way. So we never challenged the legality of Serbian sovereignty for this part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you testified the other day relating to the period following the conclusion of these agreements when you -- when you and NATO, I should say -- when NATO received information from sources, various sources, as to what was transpiring on the ground. I'd like to know if you are privy to the information that from the 16th of October, 1998, through the end of the year, December 31st, 1998, the KLA actually committed 155 distinct attacks, criminal attacks or terrorist attacks, against various persons in the territory of Kosovo-Metohija?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not aware of the precise number, and I do not remember whether we counted the incidents. But I think I stated repeatedly that I had the impression that the KLA was trying to take advantage of the Serbian withdrawal as a consequence of the 25th October agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I believe you mentioned that often the KLA would instigate incidents and then the police or Serb forces would go out in response to that, thus creating more targets for the KLA to attack. The question I have for you, sir, is if we take into account that these KLA attacks included attacks that resulted in 17 killed civilians, 31 kidnapped individuals of all ethnicities, including Serb, Albanian, Roma, and 15 wounded civilians and 15 hijacked cars, is it correct, sir, that in reality the KLA looked for targets wherever they could find them so that unless all the police and all the civilians who didn't support the KLA were removed from Kosovo, the KLA would still continue in its activities?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a conclusion which in -- based on the information I had at the time would have gone too far. But I stated repeatedly in the NATO Council that the KLA is increasingly jumping into the role of the bad guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I'd like to move on just briefly to touch on another fact you testified about, Racak. Now, as far as the incident in Racak in January 1999 is concerned, are you aware of the fact that the OSCE-KVM was informed prior to the commencement of the operation pursuant to the terms of the KVM agreement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm not entirely sure whether I was informed that they were -- that they got the information before that. Please forgive me, I don't know it precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No problem. I understand that time has passed --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- and one fact out of many can sometimes get lost in the -- in the totality of the situation. Now, irrespective of that fact, following the -- the completion of the operation, are you aware that the KLA that was present fired upon several investigative teams that were trying to get into the scene; and, therefore, the investigative teams were not able to get to the scene until January the 18th, some two days after the operation, after the bodies had been moved several times, meaning that material evidence from the -- from the on-site inspection were lost or unpreserved?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have an objection to this because we've been told we're not going to lead evidence on Racak. This is getting quite detailed. I think Mr. Ivetic is opening the door now for us to make an application to present evidence about Racak. This goes beyond the scope of what we've been trying to do in the few times that we've been to Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps that would suit him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, they called a witness which testified for several hours that talked only about Racak. And this statement here talks about going to meetings in January as a result of Racak and as a result of what Mr. Walker concluded and that is specifically what I am focusing upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I expected the objection to be a different one, which was that the factual situation is a bit more complex than you have presented. Well, let's hear what, if anything, the witness can say on this first of all; and then I'll decide whether we should explore it any further. Mr. Naumann, can you deal with that at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The one thing which I recall for sure is that Ambassador Walker did not mention to us that the KLA had fired at the KVM teams. That he did not mention in the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did -- am I correct that the information you obtained from Mr. Walker was essentially his own conclusions prior to the completion of any investigations, either by the Serb authorities or by any other groups?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he presented to us, Mr. Ivetic, his observations, his conclusions, as he had obtained them by 19th of January. And he clearly stated that these were his conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. I'd like to -- I'm done with Racak. I'd like to move on now to one final point, which just closes the issue of the October meetings again. At that point in time when you attended meetings where police officials or generals were involved, am I correct that the police officials were -- that the justifications given by the police officials and the concerns expressed by the police officials relating to Kosovo-Metohija focused primarily and solely upon the criminal activities of the KLA and other such groups?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we've heard testimony from this Commander Bislim Zyrapi during these proceedings that the KLA had approximately 17.000 to 18.000 active armed members in March of 1999. Do you recall whether such intel was available to NATO at that time?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that we had precise figures on the KLA. Since in contrast to some statements, we never regarded the KLA more or less as an ally to NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That's all the questions I have for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, there were a couple of matters in the transcript yesterday that I'm not clear on that I wanted to go back and confirm with you whether or not it's accurately recorded. At page 81, line 7, you were asked a question about -- by Mr. Ackerman. And the question was -- he was giving you an example of a military barracks housing soldiers of the enemy, even though there are numerous noncombatants there. It doesn't become a nontarget just noncombatants are present, does it? Your answer was: "A military facility -- a military barrack is, I think, a target which can be attacked. Again, the principle of avoiding unnecessary collateral damage has to be applied." And then Mr. Ackerman started to ask a question and said: "And." And then you continued your answer and said: "And we did this, Mr. Ackerman." When you say "we did this," were you referring to you attempted to avoid unnecessary collateral damage --?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- when attacking such targets?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Page 86, line 10, you were asked a question -- well, let me see if I can get this. Oh, yes, you were talking about your training when you were at the Royal College of Defence Studies, and you said: "Every one of us doing individual patrolling with a live firing rifle. Every one of us who hit a civilian target passed the course." And then you said, "so did not pass the course." Did you mean if someone hit a civilian target they failed?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 77, line 17, Mr. Ackerman raised the point to you whether or not it -- you consider it legitimate for a military commander to try and protect his own personnel when responding to hostile fire on his people. What about -- does the military commander also have an obligation to protect civilians that might be within that zone of combat?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I think I stated this clearly that he has a responsibility, and I think I went even beyond that and said that in most of our deliberations we also tried to reduce damage to opposing forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe you did say that. Thank you. I hesitate to go into this, but I do want to ask you a couple of questions about the issue Mr. Ackerman raised about bombing from 15.000 feet. You mentioned -- well, first of all, can targeting at 15.000 feet versus at 1500 feet or 150 feet, can you be as accurate from 15.000 feet with the equipment that NATO had at that time?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you use precision-guided ammunition, yes, you can be precise. It doesn't -- it really doesn't matter, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you explain for us why that is.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, if I take the example of a cruise missile being launched from a ship at a distance from 2.000 miles, you can programme the warhead in such a way that it will take a decision inflight whether it will hit this window on the left or the window to the right; and with 95 percent probability, it will hit the proper window. So I think the accuracy is mind-boggling which modern ammunitions achieved in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned that a pilot flying at 15.000 feet wouldn't necessarily be using his eyes to look at a target on the ground.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pilot flying at 150 feet would use primarily his eyes; but in all other cases, I think he would use radars and other technical devices to identify and hit the proper target.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Including overhead imagery?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only a few aircraft have this capability. They all are American. The data linking is, first of all, technically too sophisticated for many Europeans and also too expensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. One other transcript matter I wanted to be clear on. At page 86, line 19 from yesterday, there was a question about the shelling of the MUP headquarters in Belgrade. And you said: "Since it would have been one of the first attacks on down-town Belgrade, the secretary-general of NATO had to agree to that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY SAID
utterances.text: "So that must have been agreed?" You said: "At the political level." And then Judge Bonomy said: "But agreed contrary to your advice?" And your answer was: "Based upon my advice, yes." Can you tell us how that went. I understand that General Clark first proposed it to you, you asked him to go back and be sure, then what happened?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the story -- I hope not to bore Your Honours, the Court. I got the information that this headquarters should be bombed, and I first got it when -- by a colonel who was dispatched to NATO headquarters in Brussels by General Clark. And this colonel presented me with an overhead imagery of the building and its immediate surroundings, not much more than let's say 500 metres. When I saw it, I said to the colonel, Sorry, this is no basis on which I can formulate a recommendation to the secretary-general. I need additional information. I picked up the phone, called General Clark, told him what I needed, and sent the colonel back. After an hour, he came back with a bigger imagery and a map on which the surrounding -- and in particular this centre hospital was clearly visible. Then again I asked the colonel what is the -- what is the targeting? What is the amount of ammunition you want to spend on it? Got the information that I think more than a dozen cruise missiles were intended to hit this building. And when I learned this figure, I again picked up the phone, called General Clark, said, Listen, Wes, with more than a dozen cruise missiles into that building, that is presumably something which will cause a lot of collateral damage and I'm not inclined to recommend to the secretary-general to authorise such a strike. Please go back to your targeteers and look into alternative options. He called me again, this colonel still being there with the classified imagery at hand. And said, Okay, we'll change it. The -- I think he mentioned the figure six cruise missiles would be launched, and we changed the angle of attack so that collateral damage can be avoided. With that -- based on that information, I went to the secretary-general and said, This is a request of Supreme Allied Commander Europe; and based upon the modifications we discussed, I think you can go along and I would recommend you to authorise the strike. That's the full story.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Related --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One matter for the transcript which may or may not be important, 67, line 6, did I correctly hear you say that you called General Clark and said, "Listen, Wes?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, "Listen, Wes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One more matter related to that Mr. Cepic asked you some questions about that. And at page 39, line 2, today your answer you said: "When the building of the General Staff," and I think all along we had been talking about the MUP headquarters.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, Mr. Hannis, asked me two questions. One was the police headquarters, and the other one was the General Staff. Both were targets in central Belgrade, and in both cases Mr. Cepic alleged that the buildings have been evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were these two buildings close to each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honour, now you're catching me on the wrong foot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was Belgrade down-town only once in my life and that was in the middle of the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. But from what you recollect of the diagrams or the plans you were shown, can I ask you separately. You perhaps can't relate these two buildings to each other, but can I ask you separately whether the hospital was located close to the MUP headquarters or were there other buildings between them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall the imagery, the hospital was pretty close and there were no major buildings between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we show the witness Exhibit P2560 at page 14 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this concerns a question about the issue of collateral damage and mistakes made in the bombing campaign. This is a report by Lord Robertson that was done one year after Kosovo that summarised what happened, and if you could look at that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go down just slightly. Yeah, that's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The paragraph that starts above the picture. If you could start with the line that begins with the word "strikes." Could you just read that for us. Could you read that out loud?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I should read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Strikes were also complicated by the cynical Serb use of civilian homes and buildings to hide weapons and vehicles, the intermixing of military vehicles with civilian convoys, and sometimes the use of human shields." Continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One more, please.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In this way, NATO's concern to avoid civilian casualties was exploited by the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Based on your time while you were there during the NATO air campaign, is that consistent with some of the things that happened?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To hide military vehicles in civilian buildings, correct; to inter -- to mix civilian vehicles and military vehicles in convoys, correct as well; human shields, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I had wanted to ask you about something that Mr. Fila asked you about today. At page 44, line 10, he showed you the exhibit that regarded the appointment of Mr. Sainovic as President of the Yugoslav Commission for Cooperating with OSCE. When he was introduced to you at that meeting on the 24th of October, I think you said in your prior evidence that he was introduced as the man responsible for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you described that he did have some participation in the technical agreements that were worked out over the weekend of the 24th and 25th. Was it your understanding that his role regarding Kosovo was limited to cooperation with OSCE?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding when Mr. Milosevic introduced Mr. Sainovic was not that it was as limited as I read it today in this decree which I saw on the display. But I would admit, Mr. Hannis, that a head of state introducing some of his collaborators will not always use precise wording. That I have seen in many other cases as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic -- I'm sorry, Mr. Ivetic asked you a question about Mr. Walker's observations regarding Racak at page 62, lines 17 and 18 today. When you and Mr. -- You and General Clark met with Mr. Milosevic on the 19th of January, did Mr. Milosevic give you some of his observations and opinions about the events of Racak?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic -- and I think I stated this in what -- in the general statement which I made earlier on to the Milosevic case. Mr. Milosevic reacted very angrily at our allegation that Racak had been a type of a massacre. And he repeatedly stated and claimed that Serb police and military forces had acted in full accordance with Serbian law and with international law and that there was no justification whatsoever for any crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did he indicate to you -- I think it's in your written evidence. He indicated that no Serb police or military would do that crime?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Even though there was an investigation supposedly still ongoing?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an investigation going on by Serb authorities, and later on, as we learned during the day, a Finnish autopsy team was called in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Finally, I want to go to a couple of matters that Mr. Sepenuk asked you about yesterday at the very beginning of your cross-examination. He showed you a number of things from what has been referred to as the blue book that OSCE had regarding activities in Kosovo. For you in NATO, was your only sources of information about what was happening in Kosovo based on what you heard from OSCE and KDOM, or did you have other source?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had other sources as well. And for that reason, it shouldn't come to the Court as a surprise that some of the comprehensive assessments which were put on the screen yesterday did not pop up in NATO intelligence in a verbatim form. They were brought together with other pieces of information and condensed to a NATO intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what you and NATO determined as being corroborated information came from at least two member states?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: More, more. I think in -- in most cases, we had information of -- by approximately five to six member nations. And, occasionally, when I had to present the military assessment in the council, the one or the other ambassador who had not revealed its information through the intelligence channels provided additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Sepenuk at page 45 line 11 in sort of summing up the review of some of these documents from the blue book, said: "Okay. Then, General, as the year 1998 drew to a close, is it fair to say that neither the OSCE nor NATO nor Ambassador Hill nor anybody else for that matter had been successful in successfully stopping KLA provocations?" And your answer was: "Yeah, that was my impression at the time." General, at the end of 1998, had anyone been successful in stopping the Serbs from responding with disproportionate forces to those provocations?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our assessment, not. And as I think I have stated repeatedly also in yesterday's proceedings, that we were confronted with a spiral of escalation and counter-escalation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And you did talk about that spiral of escalation and counter-escalation. My last question, and I would like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 928. Your Honours, this was not a document that was on the list of exhibits to show to the witness, but I bring it to your attention in light of what has been asked in cross-examination and the challenges made. I think it is pertinent. These are minutes of the VJ collegium from the 30th of December, 1998, and there's a specific paragraph that talks about Podujevo that I would like to bring to your attention and ask General Naumann about. It's page 14 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say -- may I say that in my modest view, the Prosecution cannot present documents like this in re-direct, because they haven't announced any such thing during the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're not hearing you because of the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're just being given part of a document, and I don't know what the point of the entire document is. Why wasn't it shown in good time? This document is not derived from the cross-examination really. I really don't know what this is all about. I wish I could have seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is important to you, Mr. Hannis, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Naumann, I wonder if you could briefly leave the room with the usher while we deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the issue that this relates to, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this relates to the Podujevo incident you heard Colonel Ciaglinski and General DZ speak about, which was viewed as a violation of the October agreements. The Serb side presented it as they were engaged in winter exercises with some of their armoured units, that they were then fired upon by the KLA, and they were only responding to that. General Naumann has been asked about that in cross-examination about disproportionate use of force, about who initiated all the contacts. And here we have in the VJ collegium, of which General Ojdanic was the head, there is a discussion about this. General Dimitrijevic is the one speaking here. He was the head of the intelligence service for the General Staff. And he is describing what appears to be that this was genuinely not a planned exercise, but rather a means of drawing the KLA into firing upon them so the MUP could go in and take action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is your question for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask him if -- well, Your Honour, basically I just want to put this document in to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not appropriate in this way, Mr. Hannis. If there is a witness who is going to introduce this document or going to be introduced in some other way, fine. But you're going to put a proposition from a document to the witness who has already said he has no knowledge of Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that's correct, Your Honour. He did indicate that he believed Podujevo was one of the ten incidents that was described in the list that they gave to Mr. Milosevic when they went on the 19th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, but he's got no knowledge of what happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This doesn't comply with any rule that had been followed in this case. It's a document that will have to be introduced in an appropriate way and not simply by asking a witness, who's got no connection with it and no particular knowledge of the events, a question which is designed just to introduce the statement in the document itself. So that's not the right way to deal with this, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I'll accept that. I would indicate, though, that we think it's appropriate as a contextual document at this time to consider this witness's evidence as to who was initiating and responding to armed conflict and as a contextual document for Colonel Ciaglinski and General DZ and their evidence about Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're going to have to re-consider how you will introduce the document, because we will not allow this witness to be asked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we would offer it from the bench, Your Honour, because this is something we received in response to an RFA from the Government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I wasn't aware you just received it. When did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure of the date we received it. I can find that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't doubt that it may be a relevant document, but I don't think this moment at the end of this witness's evidence is the time and context for the introduction of this document. You will have to consider, again. Sorry, Mr. Visnjic, do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let us just clarify two matters. First of all, the Prosecution has this documentation. They have had it for at least a year as far as I know. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you want to persuade us to allow it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you'd be well advised to sit down now. You will have to find an appropriate witness to deal with this, Mr. Hannis, or make an appropriate submission about it, and that I think in view of the nature of this document would be a written submission. But this is not the -- you have not identified in relation to this witness something that he could from his own experience deal with in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand. I think -- I'll check but I believe this document was part of a prior submission, a written submission, of evidence to the Court which was initially denied. We feel that it is something which does not necessarily need to come in through a particular witness. The VJ collegium minutes are a collection we received pursuant to an RFA. They're relevant to a number of matters, and we -- I propose to bring this one up at this time, because I think it related to Ciaglinski, DZ, and this witness and the Podujevo incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But are you saying that this document was among the documents you invited us to admit as stand-alone documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did that decision not refuse to admit them without prejudice?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, therefore, a circumstance has developed plainly it may turn out to be appropriate to admit something. And I think that you ought to reflect on whether simply presenting it orally is the right way to try to do that now that you can contextualise the elements in this document that you seek to rely on and perhaps establish its authenticity, then the position may well be quite different from what it was before. But it needs to be done in an orderly fashion and notice needs to be given to the Defence to enable them to respond appropriate so that we get full submissions on something that could turn out to be pretty important.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So in the present circumstances we will refuse to allow the question that you intended to ask, since it does not appear to us to be a question that the witness could provide us with an informed answer on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Before we have the witness back in, I just want to indicate with some of these collections what I would call all-encompassing collections that pertain to a number of matters and a number of witnesses, it is a dilemma for us somewhat to try to put in a part of a document or one document of many when there is a witness that touches on some particular aspect, or try and put the whole collection in at the end and then try to relate back to Your Honours things that have happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I hope we've tried to give guidance on that already. The motion to which you've referred was a motion inviting us to admit material without really seeing how it would fit into the case, and we admitted what was obvious to us as relevant material and also authentic material. In making any further submission for the admission of documents standing alone, you should be directing the Trial Chamber's attention to the passages that are relevant to the case and to the question how they are relevant to the case. Now, it's for you in making that submission to judge in your own mind whether the whole of the document also needs to be admitted to enable a full understanding of the situation to be given to the trial. But please bear in mind that we -- I don't know whether it's been the practice in the past or not, but we are not prepared to accept large volumes of material that might later feature in an argument that has later been put together. This case has been on the go so long that the parties ought to know exactly what their case is and where documents fit into it, and we expect to be assisted in that way. Now, that's the best guidance I can give you. If you take the view that you will throw material at us because it might be relevant in view of the heading, then you're making a big mistake. And, indeed, we will reject it and may in fact as a result of that miss the nuggets that are in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may take one more minute of your time, Your Honour, because this is difficult. In another case I was on, there was an accused who was head of the legislature, and we put in Assembly sessions which had a lot of stuff which was of no interest. But to try and present a fair picture of the parts that we wanted to argue about and to deal with what was probably a legitimate Defence complaint if we select that paragraph or that page, we may not be giving you a fair picture. I know it then falls upon the Court to perhaps have to wade through some stuff that is not relevant, but it is really difficult to single out a page or a paragraph from a large collection like that. And sometimes it's the tone of the entire meeting and the participants that take on some importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you may be right about that, but you would have to in your submission say that that's the case and give examples of why that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is not the job of this Trial Chamber to simply receive material and decide for itself where there might be something relevant to the case. The parties should be making submissions about the relevance of the material for the Trial Chamber to consider before deciding the quantity that requires to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for your patience and your guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it is helpful to have these discussions in an appropriate context, and I'm grateful to you for explaining your position. But I do think that it sounds as though a lot of work has to be done by you on material which could turn out to be of some importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we can have the witness back in, and I'll have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Unless anyone wishes to comment that our approach that we've indicated ought to be modified in some way. All right. Let's have the witness back, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, we've disallowed that question. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Naumann, I have no further questions for you. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, Your Honour. It is my impression that in the re-direct, a new topic was opened. My learned friend, Mr. Hannis, made use of a document by Lord Robertson, marked P2560. And he used it to put a question concerning the use of civilian facilities and columns of vehicles and the use of the Serb forces of the aforementioned instances. It is at page 69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it was a matter that arose out of cross-examination. It's an issue of collateral damage. Now, what is your concern?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even the two buildings that I mentioned, gathering from the witness's answer and the way the question was put, I gathered from it that there was some military vehicles hidden there in the MUP and the General Staff building; therefore, it remains open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you understood the witness to be saying there were military vehicles in the MUP and General Staff buildings. Is that right? But they are military -- well, they are police and General Staff buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stated something to the contrary during cross-examination, and the witness said that he wasn't familiar with the fact that all -- that both buildings had been evacuated. There were no people or vehicles in them. But if the Bench is happy with such an answer, then I will withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you know our position is to refer to documents only to the extent that they've been introduced into the evidence, and silence might have been your appropriate course of action. But now you've raised something in the document that we could hardly ignore, which we probably would not have paid any attention to. But now that you've raised it, I suppose we have no alternative but to allow you to ask questions, so please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumann, it is I, again. I have already introduced myself to you. My learned friend, Mr. Hannis, asked you something about the targeting of facilities including a MUP building and a General Staff building. You said you were not familiar with the information that these two buildings had been targeted. My interest here is the use of civilian facilities and columns of vehicles by the MUP and the VJ. During the bombing, you gained such information via satellite pictures, since you did not have people in the field. You did not have any observers on the ground, did you, Mr. Naumann?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. Cepic, I think I need to clarify a slight confusion which obviously occurred. The question which I got from Mr. Hannis did not refer to the VJ -- or to the VJ General Staff or the police headquarters. In the -- with regard to these two targets, I remain with my statement which I made earlier on. I was not aware of the evacuation, and I did not allege in these proceedings that any military vehicles or something like this were hidden in these two buildings. I think it would also physically have been impossible, unless there was an underground garage of which I do not know. What Mr. Hannis was referring to is that Lord Robertson stated in his report one year after the Kosovo air campaign that during the campaign, the VJ used civilian buildings to hide military vehicles and also mixed civilian and military vehicles in convoys. That is something which I have seen and I confirmed. And I clearly said I do not know -- I do not remember any use of human beings as human shields. So I think we should keep these two things separate. What you asked me about was the two targets in down-town Belgrade and what Mr. Hannis talked about was the conduct of the operations in the Kosovo province.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Cepic, that in the document P2560, there is reference to vehicles being hidden in the MUP and General Staff building?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Perhaps I misunderstood the answer, and I may have been wrong. Nonetheless, I wanted to seek this clarification. My further question would be, although it might be too complex, but it pertains to the assertion from the document that NATO gained information about the situation on the ground via satellites. That was the question I posed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm happy to answer that question. Well, of course we gained information via satellite, Mr. Cepic, satellite imagery, but we have also other instruments to gain pictures. The drones were already mentioned. There were other manned aircraft who were taking photographs. So I think we had a number of instruments which allowed us to get some pictorial evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Naumann. With His Honour's leave, I have one more question. There were mistakes in conclusions made from such pictures, such as was the case of the two convoys mentioned by Mr. Ackerman in Bistrazin and Korisa. In total, almost 200 civilians were killed in those actions. That would be my last question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. That goes beyond the scope of what you were permitted to do, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise for having interrupted and I thank you for this possibility to pose additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Mr. Naumann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, how common is the writing of books by senior military officers involved in modern-day conflict?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, it's getting increasingly popular, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a reason for it that you can detect?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it depends very much on personalities and on the situation in the individual country. If I -- if I had to do something like this, I would not write a book about an individual campaign. I've written a book which reflects my experience in the situation after the Cold War, and I tried to formulate an assessment of the situation as I see it in order to contribute to the strategic discussion in my country. But I would never do something like this on, let's say, on the experiences gained in operations like such in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do they sell well, these books?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But, again, this is different from country to country. And in the United States of America, you can presumably sell such books. In Europe, I think if you write books about stories concerning so-called celebrities in the public life, you will get a lot of money, but not if you talk about military or security policies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's also increasingly common among politicians.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is something special about it, and I have -- fortunately, I was -- or unfortunately during the last ten years of my military career, I witnessed a couple of traumatic changes in European history. And when I now read some of the memoirs written by well-known German politicians, I can state that my recollection of some details is quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not been a feature of this case, but in other cases of course before this Tribunal the books written by various people in former Yugoslavia have been of a similar nature where both political and military combat issues are addressed. Anyway, I think that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give it. You can rest assured that we will consider carefully all you've said and also everything you've said in the past in the Tribunal, which has been presented to us. You're now free to leave. That may complete your involvement in the Tribunal; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any surprises, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what surprises, Your Honour, but we have no further witnesses to call before the winter recess, Your Honour. We -- we will be filing our updated witness list I think later today or tomorrow. I think you'll see that our total number of witnesses is less than it was when we first filed our witness list back in May or in July. So I think we're on course to hopefully finish with our case in chief sometime in March or April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's encouraging.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can't guarantee that, Your Honour, because I don't know exactly how long cross-exam will go and sometimes other matters that will come up, but I think we have something in the neighbourhood of 35 new witnesses in the new year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The sitting schedule we have for the new year, I can outline just now. When we come back and recommence on the 16th of January, we'll be sitting mornings for that week. The week of the 22nd, we aim to sit according to the schedule we would have had this week but for all five days. That's a 9.00 to 3.30 schedule. That's followed by a routine week. I can't tell you whether it's mornings or afternoons the 29th of January. The 5th of February, we will not sit. But on the week the 6th of February, we'll be sitting for full days; that's the 9.00 to 3.30 slot on the Wednesday to the Friday. The final arrangement for the 6th is not yet made; and we'll, as we did on one previous occasion, we'll run the longer sitting over into the Monday of the following week, that's the 12th of February. The rest of that week we'll be sitting half days. The 19th of February, week beginning the 19th, will be the full-day schedule, the 9.00 to 3.30. The 26th will be the half-day schedule. The 5th of March we will not sit. And from the 6th until the 12th, that's the 12th, the Monday, we will sit on the longer schedule from 9.00 to 3.30. Of course, that's subject to adjustment, and indeed may be impeded by other cases that get underway in the interim. The programme for the overall Tribunal is uncertain. All I'm indicating is our plans so we can avoid what happened this week. The events of today rather confirm that the recess is arriving at an opportune time. The Chamber has appreciated counsels' efforts in recent weeks to maintain focus on the significant relevant issues, and, indeed, we were discussing the matter only yesterday. And that effort seems to have been led by the senior members of the Defence teams and responded to by the others. So we welcome that. We hope that over the recess you will all find peaceful time, and we hope also that the recess will allow you to recharge your batteries and return refreshed for the next leg, which may not be as arduous as the first one in light of what Mr. Hannis has said. But there again, you never know in this place. So we will adjourn now, and we will resume at 9.00 on the 16th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of January, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
